subject: geography
title: Cultural Globalisation, Gender and Identity
welcome_lead: K-pop fans in Brazil, hijab fashion in Indonesia, World Cup in Qatar — explore the cultural dimensions of global interactions.
meta_desc: Geography HL Adventure: cultural globalisation, gender and identity.
final_note: You have heard global culture as conversation, not just diffusion. Identity is co-produced in motion.

concepts.def: Spread of cultural elements (language, food, religion) from one society to another.
Mixing of cultural influences producing new forms, e.g. Tex-Mex cuisine, Afrobeats.
Dominance, often economic and cultural, of one group or country over others (Gramsci).

walkthroughs.body_html: Cultural globalisation involves the flow of films, music, sport, religion, food and clothing. US, European, East Asian and increasingly African cultural products travel globally — Korean Wave (Hallyu), Bollywood, Nollywood. Critics fear homogenisation; others emphasise hybridity and active reception.

Joseph Nye's 'soft power' concept emphasises culture, values and policies as sources of attraction. The US, UK, France, South Korea, Japan and China deploy soft power through universities, scholarships, broadcasting (BBC, CGTN) and global brands.

Globalisation has accelerated debates about gender and identity: education for girls (Malala Fund), migration and care chains, LGBTQ+ rights and backlash, hybrid identities in diaspora communities. The UN's GII and Global Gender Gap Report measure progress, revealing both progress and entrenched inequalities.

options: A process where warming triggers changes that cause more warming — e.g. melting Arctic ice exposes dark ocean, which absorbs more heat, melting more ice (ice-albedo feedback).
